glossary.definition: Access to the systems engineers use (GitHub, GitLab, Salesforce, Snowflake, Databricks, Google Workspace) that is requested, approved, time-bound and removed automatically, with a receipt for every grant. Ping release claim, UNVERIFIED on our tenant.

A policy has one to three approval levels; each level is a role (the manager, the resource owner, the security group, the data owner) routed to automatically. Approvers act directly from Slack or Mattermost; Teams, Jira and ServiceNow only receive notifications and tickets. The roles, the depth limit and how each resolves to a person are the lab's own reading. Ping release claim, UNVERIFIED on our tenant.

The person who made a request cannot approve it, an agent cannot approve anything, and an expired request cannot be approved. In the lab self-approval is not a setting: no policy edit can switch it off. Ping release claim, UNVERIFIED on our tenant.
aliases: approver cannot approve their own request

glossary.definition: A policy can approve a request by itself when its level and window fit a rule (enabled, up to a level, up to a number of minutes). The decision is recorded as made by the policy. The rule's shape is lab-invented. Ping release claim, UNVERIFIED on our tenant.

Every grant carries an expiry. A reaper reconciles continuously and removes access from the platform when the window closes, even if the original grant workflow is long finished. In the lab it wakes every 5 lab minutes and at the end of every clock move (lab-invented). Ping release claim, UNVERIFIED on our tenant.

Every grant is recorded. The lab chains its receipts (each hashes its own fields and the hash of the one before, and a count and head hash are kept beside them) so editing, reordering or dropping receipts is detected; without a key or an external anchor, someone who can rewrite both can forge the chain. The product's receipt format is not public, so all of this is LAB-INVENTED. Ping release claim, UNVERIFIED on our tenant.

When several policies grant the same access to the same subject, the grants are reference-counted: the platform keeps the access, at the highest level any of them gives, until the last one ends. Removing one policy must not remove access another still grants. Ping release claim, UNVERIFIED on our tenant.

Every grant is reconciled against the platform nightly to surface access granted outside Privilege. The lab flags four kinds (unrecorded, elevated, missing, reduced); the kinds, the 02:00 lab-clock time and the remediation are lab-invented. Ping release claim, UNVERIFIED on our tenant.

glossary.term: One model for people and agents
glossary.definition: An engineer asking for a warehouse role and an agent asking for a peer's capability are the same request, approval, expiry and revoke cycle, recorded the same way in one audit trail: the difference is only the subject. Ping release claim, UNVERIFIED on our tenant.
A clock the visitor advances (+15 minutes, +1 hour, +1 day) so expiry, the reaper and the nightly reconcile can be seen. It only moves forward. Lab-invented.

The console schema (2026-10-31, schema only) gives Hitl to the Slack integration, the Jira project and the ServiceNow table, and Sync to the Databricks, Salesforce and Snowflake account objects. The lab uses them as switches (where approval requests go; whether the reconcile reads a platform): how they behave in the product is not known. Ping release claim, UNVERIFIED on our tenant.

cards.label: Scenario 1: An engineer asks for a warehouse role
cards.description: Two approval levels route to the data owner and then to the security group; every grant carries an expiry; the reaper removes the role when the window closes.

cards.label: Scenario 2: Self-approval is refused
cards.description: lee.park asks for access during a payments settlement incident and tries to approve their own request. The lab refuses, and says why. A colleague in the security group approves.

cards.label: Scenario 3: Low-risk access is approved by policy
cards.description: Read access for up to two hours is approved by the policy itself, recorded as such, and still removed on time.

cards.label: Scenario 4: Two policies grant the same access
cards.description: A routine write grant and an incident grant overlap on the same repository. When the shorter one ends, the access stays, because the other policy still grants it. It goes only when the last reference does.

cards.label: Scenario 5: An agent and an engineer, one model
cards.description: An agent asks for a Unity Catalog privilege and an engineer asks for the same one. Same policy, same approval, same receipt, one audit trail: the only difference is the subject.

cards.label: Scenario 6: Access granted outside Privilege
cards.description: Someone grants access by hand on the platform. The reconcile finds it, a nightly run finds it again, and the reaper cannot remove it because it was never a grant.

cards.label: Approve as the wrong person
cards.description: Act as the requester, an agent or someone not routed to the level: the lab refuses and says why.

cards.label: Move the lab clock
cards.description: Advance +15 minutes, +1 hour or +1 day and watch the reaper remove the access and the receipts chain.

cards.label: Change a platform by hand
cards.description: Grant access outside Privilege, then reconcile: the finding names the platform, the person and the level.

cards.label: Why it matters: SaaS Access Management (slide 51)
cards.description: Challenge: standing access accumulates and nobody can say who still holds what; audit findings on standing access stall the review. Technical: request, approve, expire, revoke as one cycle across six platforms, with a reaper and nightly drift detection. Business: standing-access audit findings close without manual clean-up: lower risk, less compliance effort, and the same JIT model as agents. These are Ping claims, unverified on our tenant.
